//: Starting-point permissions for Claude Code in a ct workspace. The session runs in auto mode: a classifier reads every action that no rule settles, lets routine work through, and refuses what destroys work, touches production or leaves the trust boundary, unless the person asked for exactly that. So nothing here asks. An `ask` rule prompts where the classifier would have decided, and it wins over every allow rule and hook: measured over four weeks on one machine, the rules this template used to ship (rm, kill, kubectl and helm mutations, destructive git) raised 1300 prompts, of which the person refused three. install.sh removes them from an existing file (templates/retired-ask-rules.txt lists them) and keeps any rule its owner added. `autoMode.classifyAllShell` sends every shell command to the classifier while auto mode is active, whatever any allow list says. Without it an allow rule settles a command before the classifier runs, and a rule wider than one exact command lets through what the classifier is there to judge: `Bash(direnv exec *)`, one "don't ask again" away in any workspace, allows `direnv exec . kubectl delete ...` unseen. So in auto mode the `allow` list below spares nothing and costs nothing; it is for the other modes, and holds reads and `git add`. Three reads it used to hold are gone because even there they are not only reads: `helm template` runs a program with `--post-renderer`, `kubectl kustomize` with `--enable-exec`, and `kubectl config view --raw` prints credentials. Outside auto mode (accept-edits, manual) Claude Code prompts for every command that no allow rule covers, with or without ask rules. `deny` is a hard stop for `rm -rf /` itself (a `*` matches any characters, so `rm -rf /*` would deny every absolute-path `rm -rf`). `autoMode` tells the classifier what a ct workspace is: `$defaults` keeps Claude Code's own entries, and a site adds its organisation, remotes, clusters and registries beside the entries here, which are labelled `(ct)`. ct-scratch-guard, a hook install.sh registers, allows a command that is nothing but rm inside a workspace .scratch/. Copy to ~/.claude/settings.json and add your own path grants (Edit/Write/Read roots, permissions.additionalDirectories), deliberately not included here.

environment: **Workspace layout (ct)**: The agent starts in a ct workspace directory, `<root>/<workspace>/` (for example `~/dev/agent-a/`), which is not itself a git repository. It holds one full git clone per repository the agent works on, each with its own remote(s), plus the agent's own `.scratch/` and `.claude/plans/` directories. Every clone directly inside the agent's own workspace, with that clone's configured remote(s), is a Trusted repo exactly as if the session had started inside it, and the whole workspace directory is project scope. Other workspaces under the same root belong to other agents: reading them is fine, changing or deleting their files is not a local operation.
allow: Workspace Scratch Cleanup (ct): Deleting files and directories under the agent's own workspace `.scratch/` directory (`<root>/<workspace>/.scratch/`), by literal path, glob or recursive delete, is the routine cleanup the workspace conventions require of every agent, whichever session created them. It is not Irreversible Local Destruction. This does NOT cover a delete whose target is a variable the transcript never assigns (see Unverifiable Deletion Target), another workspace's `.scratch/`, or `.scratch` reached through a symlink.

Own Unpushed Commits (ct): In a ct workspace each clone is worked in by one agent (other agents have clones of their own), and a conversation runs for days and is summarised along the way, so the `git commit` that made HEAD is often no longer visible in the transcript. In a clone inside the agent's own workspace (a submodule checkout included), `git commit --amend` of a commit that is not yet on the remote, followed by `git pull --rebase` and an ordinary push, is the agent reshaping its own work: the normal iteration loop that Git Destructive leaves alone. A `git commit` missing from the transcript is not a sign that HEAD is someone else's. This does NOT cover any force-push, amending or rebasing commits that are already on the remote branch, a clone outside the agent's own workspace, or discarding working-tree changes (`git reset --hard`, `git checkout -- .`, `git clean`, `git stash drop`).
